flashcards.front: Distinguish Cache Penetration, Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd), and Cache Avalanche.
flashcards.back: Penetration: queries for non-existent keys miss cache and hit DB (fix: Bloom filter or null-caching). Stampede: 1 hot key expires under heavy concurrency (fix: Singleflight coalescing / soft TTL). Avalanche: many keys expire at once or Redis crashes (fix: jittered TTLs + cluster HA).

flashcards.front: What is the main risk of Write-Behind (Write-Back) caching compared to Write-Through?
flashcards.back: Write-Behind acks writes after updating Redis and flushes asynchronously to the database in batches, risking permanent data loss if the cache node crashes before flushing.

quizzes.scenario: Bots request millions of random product ids that do not exist. Redis misses every time, so all of the attack traffic reaches Postgres.
quizzes.question: Which defense stops this cache penetration with the least memory?
options: More aggressive LRU eviction so Redis frees memory faster
Read replicas so Postgres can absorb the extra lookups
Longer TTLs on existing keys so fewer requests miss
A shared Bloom filter of valid ids, updated on every create
quizzes.explanation: A Bloom filter has no false negatives for keys that were added, so a 'not present' answer can return 404 without touching Postgres. It must be shared (or updated on every write) so new keys are visible to every pod. Short-TTL negative caching is the simpler alternative when the key space is small.
optionExplanations: Eviction policy does not help; the attacked keys were never in the cache.
Replicas add capacity but still pay for every bogus query; attackers scale cheaper.
The misses are for keys that do not exist, so TTLs on real keys change nothing.
Correct. Unknown ids are rejected before the database, and new ids stay visible.

quizzes.scenario: At midnight, 500,000 homepage items that were cached together at noon all reach their 12-hour TTL at once, and the database falls over.
quizzes.question: What is this failure, and what prevents it?
options: A cache avalanche; add random jitter to each TTL
Cache penetration; add a Bloom filter in front of the DB
A hot key; replicate the homepage key across shards
Write-behind data loss; switch the cache to write-through
quizzes.explanation: Many keys expiring together is a cache avalanche. Adding random jitter to each TTL (for example 12 h plus up to 30 min) spreads the refills out over time.
optionExplanations: Correct. Jitter spreads expiries so refills arrive gradually.
Penetration is about keys that do not exist. These keys exist and expired together.
There is no single hot key here; it is half a million keys expiring at once.
The write policy is unrelated; the problem is synchronized expiry on reads.

quizzes.scenario: A flash-sale key expires while 8,000 requests per second for it arrive, spread across 40 app pods. Each pod runs Singleflight, which collapses duplicate in-flight fetches inside one process.
quizzes.question: About how many database queries does the refill cause, and how do you get it to one?
options: About 200, one per database connection in the pool
Exactly 1, because Singleflight coalesces across the fleet
About 40, one per pod; add a shared SET NX refresh lease
About 8,000, because Singleflight only works for writes
quizzes.explanation: Singleflight works per process, so each of the 40 pods still sends its own query. A fleet-wide refresh lease (SET key NX PX) lets one pod refill while others serve a slightly stale value, and probabilistic early refresh avoids the synchronized expiry in the first place.
optionExplanations: Connection count caps concurrency, but coalescing already cut it to one per pod.
Singleflight state lives in each process's memory; other pods cannot see it.
Correct. Per-process coalescing stops at the pod boundary.
Singleflight coalesces reads well; it simply cannot cross pod boundaries.
